screens.title: Understanding User Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Every action on a Linux system happens on behalf of a user. User accounts give each person or service a unique identity so the kernel can enforce permissions, log activity, and allocate resources. In this chapter you will learn how user accounts are defined, how the system maps human names to numerical IDs, and why sensitive data is separated into more secure files. We will examine the canonical /etc/passwd entry, explain each colon-separated field, and contrast that file with /etc/shadow where encrypted password hashes live. You will also learn how UIDs and GIDs drive ownership and permission checks, why system accounts use special shells like /sbin/nologin, and where personal configuration files live in a home directory. By the end you will be able to read a passwd line, interpret UID/GID ownership, locate common dotfiles, and decide whether an account is a system service account or a regular user. Think about one account on your system you can inspect safely; this chapter helps you understand what each field means and how to interpret ownership across systems.

screens.title: Why user accounts exist
screens.narratorSegment: A Linux user account is a system identity used to run commands, own files, and access resources. The account ties a human or service to a set of rights and a workspace, so every change can be attributed and access can be enforced. This matters because the kernel evaluates actions by UID and GID, not by username text. If accounts are poorly managed, auditing is harder and unauthorized actions can go unnoticed. A concrete example is creating a file: the file is recorded with numerical owner and group identifiers; when another system lacks the same user ID, the file owner may display only as a number. A common misconception is that the username alone governs permissions; in fact the kernel only uses the numerical ID. Another confusion is treating system service accounts like regular users; many service accounts have restricted shells to prevent interactive login. Takeaway: treat user accounts as auditable identities—use distinct administrative accounts for people, reserve system accounts for services, and inspect UID/GID when diagnosing ownership issues. Which account will you inspect first to confirm ownership on your host?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Why user accounts exist
Definition
User account as system identity
An account provides a unique identity used for permission checks, ownership, and audit trails. It is the foundational unit of security and resource management on Linux.
Concrete example
When you create a file, the filesystem records the creating process's UID and primary GID. If you copy that file to another host that lacks the same UID mapping, the owner may appear as a number instead of a username.
Common misconception
People often assume the username alone defines permissions. In reality, the kernel uses UID and GID numerically; names are conveniences resolved from system files.
Scenario
Auditing a file copied between systems
If you see ownership shown as UID 1005, check /etc/passwd on both systems. Either create the user with the same UID on the destination, or change ownership to a local user with chown.
Key Takeaway

Treat accounts as auditable identities; prefer separate human admin accounts and reserve service accounts for automated processes.

Common mistake

Using a system service account for human logins increases the attack surface and breaks expected privilege separation.

screens.title: Reading /etc/passwd
screens.narratorSegment: The /etc/passwd file is a plain-text table listing each account on the system. Each line has seven colon-separated fields that describe the account metadata. Let's walk through the canonical example line: johndoe:x:1001:1001:John Doe,,,:/home/johndoe:/bin/bash. The username is the login label you type. The second field is typically an x placeholder indicating password hashes live in /etc/shadow. The third field is the UID, the numerical identity the kernel uses. The fourth is the primary GID, tying the account to a default group. The fifth field, the GECOS or comment field, stores optional human-readable information like full name and contact. The sixth field sets the user's home directory and the seventh sets the login shell. A concrete step to practice is grep "$(whoami)" /etc/passwd and then explain each field aloud. A common misunderstanding is expecting sensitive data in passwd; instead, only a placeholder appears because the real secret is stored in the root-only shadow file. End by asking: can you name the seven fields for your account and explain the role of the UID? Reading /etc/passwd means seven fields: username, password placeholder, uid, gid, gecos, home directory, login shell — all colon-separated.. In practical terms, understand each colon-separated field with a real example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Reading /etc/passwd
Walkthrough
Sample entry
johndoe:x:1001:1001:John Doe,,,:/home/johndoe:/bin/bash
Username
Login label used as a convenience; kernel uses UID.
Password placeholder
Usually an x indicating the hash is in /etc/shadow.
UID
Numerical identity used internally for permissions.
GID
Primary group numeric ID applied to new files.
GECOS, Home, Shell
GECOS is a comment field for full name and contact. Home directory is the user's workspace. Login shell defines the interactive interpreter or may be /sbin/nologin for non-interactive accounts.
Exercise

Run: grep "$(whoami)" /etc/passwd and identify each field. Note the placeholder and then, with sudo, inspect /etc/shadow only if needed.

Key Takeaway

Memorize the seven fields and the role of the placeholder to avoid exposing sensitive password hashes.

screens.title: UIDs, GIDs, and permission checks
screens.narratorSegment: UIDs and GIDs are core to how Linux enforces file permissions. When you open or modify a file, the kernel checks the process's effective UID and groups against the file's owner UID and group GID. If the effective UID matches the file owner, owner permissions apply; otherwise, if any of the process groups match the file group, group permissions apply; if neither, the world permissions apply. Concretely, run id to see your UID and supplementary groups; then create a simple file and observe ownership with ls -l. A common pitfall is assuming username strings are authoritative; ownership is numeric and the mapping to names depends on local /etc/passwd entries. Another scenario: you copy files between hosts and see only numeric owners. To resolve this, either recreate the same UID/GID on the destination or chown the files to existing users. Takeaway: always reason about numbers — UIDs and GIDs — when diagnosing permission mismatches. How would you fix a file owned by UID 1005 on a new host? UIDs, GIDs, and permission checks means kernel compares process uid/gids to file uid/gid values; names are resolved only for display.. In practical terms, how numerical ids determine ownership and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Kernel compares process UID/GIDs to file UID/GID values; names are resolved only for display.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › UIDs, GIDs, and permission checks
Process
Permission evaluation steps
  1. Kernel checks process effective UID vs file owner UID.
  2. If not owner, kernel checks process group list vs file GID.
  3. If no match, kernel applies world (other) permissions.
Concrete example
Run id to list numeric IDs, create a file, then ls -l to see UID/GID mapping. If names are missing on another host, the kernel still enforces numeric ownership.
Scenario — transferred file
If a file shows owner 1005 on the new system, either create devuser with UID 1005 and group GID 1005, or chown to an existing user to restore readable ownership names.
Key Takeaway

Always inspect numeric IDs when diagnosing permissions — names are presentation only.

Pitfall

Assuming username text is authoritative can mislead troubleshooting after system migrations.

screens.title: System accounts vs regular user accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Linux distinguishes system accounts created for services from regular human user accounts. System accounts typically have UIDs below 1000 and are used by daemons like apache or mysql. They often have non-interactive shells such as /bin/nologin or /sbin/nologin to prevent direct login. Regular user accounts typically start at 1000 (or 500 on some distributions) and have home directories and interactive shells like /bin/bash. A practical example: an account with UID 2 or UID 0 is a system account; root is UID 0 and has full privileges. A common mistake is enabling interactive login for a service account; this increases risk and complicates audits. When you see a passwd entry with /sbin/nologin, understand it is intended for automated processes rather than human sessions. Takeaway: maintain strict separation—create separate regular administrator accounts for people and keep service accounts constrained. Which accounts on your system have shells set to nologin, and why were they configured that way? System accounts vs regular user accounts means system accounts (uids usually <1000) run services and use non-interactive shells; regular users have interactive shells and home directories.. In practical terms, uid ranges, shells, and intended use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › System accounts vs regular
Comparison
System accounts
  • UIDs typically below 1000
  • Non-interactive shells like /sbin/nologin
  • Created for daemons and services
Regular users
  • UIDs usually start at 1000 or 500
  • Have home directories and interactive shells
  • Intended for human administrators and users
Practical check

Run: grep -E ":/s?bin/nologin$" /etc/passwd to find accounts blocked from interactive login.

Example entry
backup:x:500:500:Backup User:/var/backups:/sbin/nologin
This indicates an account intended for automated backups and not for human login. It reduces attack surface.
Key Takeaway

Do not reuse system accounts for human administration; create distinct regular accounts instead.

screens.title: Home directories and dotfiles
screens.narratorSegment: A user's home directory, usually /home/username, is the personal workspace where files and configuration live. Hidden dotfiles like. bashrc,. profile, and. vimrc customize the shell and applications when a user logs in. Inspecting these files helps you troubleshoot environment problems or unexpected behavior. For example,. bashrc may set prompt customization and PATH additions;. profile can set environment variables that apply to login shells. A practical step is cd ~ and ls -a to list hidden files, then open a dotfile to note export statements or aliases. A common misconception is that dotfiles are system-wide; they are per-user and only affect that user's environment unless copied into /etc/profile or skeleton directories. As an administrator, you may need to check dotfiles when a user reports a broken shell or missing command. Takeaway: know where user-specific settings live and how they are applied during login so you can quickly diagnose environment issues. Home directory purpose
The home directory is a user's personal file tree and default working directory after login; it stores documents, configuration, and application data.

screens.title: Inspecting user information with commands
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few essential commands for inspecting your account and mapping numeric IDs. whoami prints your current username; id shows your UID, primary GID, and supplementary groups. Use grep "$(whoami)" /etc/passwd to display the passwd entry for your account. These commands give you both the human-readable name and the numeric IDs you need to reason about ownership and permissions. For example, after running id you might see uid=1001(johndoe) gid=1001(johndoe) groups=1001(johndoe),27(sudo). This tells you your numeric identity and that you are a member of the sudo group. A common trap is reading only names and ignoring the numeric values; always note the UID when diagnosing ownership. When you need to inspect the encrypted password entry, use sudo grep "$(whoami)" /etc/shadow but do so carefully—shadow contains hashes and should not be shared. Takeaway: these commands form a fast inspection workflow to answer who owns a file and what groups a user belongs to. Inspecting user information with commands means use whoami, id, and grep to map the username to numeric uid/gid values and verify group memberships.. In practical terms, whoami, id, and grep to quickly map account details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Why /etc/shadow exists
screens.narratorSegment: Historically, /etc/passwd contained password hashes, but storing secrets in a file world-readable by many processes posed a security risk. The current model places a placeholder in passwd and keeps encrypted password hashes in /etc/shadow which is only readable by root. This prevents unprivileged processes or users from reading password hashes and attempting offline attacks. A concrete practice is never to cat or share /etc/shadow output; use sudo only when required for administrative tasks that need shadow fields, such as password aging checks. A common misconception is that the x in /etc/passwd means no password; instead, it signals that the hash is stored securely elsewhere. When auditing accounts, check for unexpected permissions on these files—/etc/passwd should be readable system-wide for name resolution, while /etc/shadow must remain restricted. Takeaway: protecting hashed secrets reduces attack surface; always treat /etc/shadow as sensitive root-only data. Why /etc/shadow exists means the 'x' placeholder in passwd points to /etc/shadow where encrypted password hashes are kept under root-only permissions.. In practical terms, separating password hashes from public account metadata. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Resolving ownership after file migration
screens.narratorSegment: When files are copied between systems, ownership can appear as numeric UIDs and GIDs if the destination lacks matching names. This happens because Linux stores ownership as numbers, and name resolution depends on local /etc/passwd and /etc/group entries. You have two correct options: recreate the user and group with the same UID and GID on the destination, or change ownership to a local user using chown and chgrp. Recreating the account preserves intended ownership semantics for multi-user environments; chowning is simple when the original user no longer exists. A concrete workflow: check the numeric owner with ls -n to see numbers, inspect /etc/passwd on both systems to compare mappings, then decide whether to add a user with useradd --uid or run chown recursively. A common mistake is to rename users without preserving UIDs, which does not fix numeric ownership. Takeaway: always check numeric IDs first, then choose recreate or chown based on whether the original account should exist on the new system. Resolving ownership after file migration means if ownership displays as numbers, either recreate corresponding uid/gid entries on the host or chown files to local accounts.. In practical terms, options when you encounter numeric owners on a new system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Security practices for accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Handling user accounts securely involves a few simple rules. First, treat /etc/shadow as sensitive: only root should read it, and you should not share its contents. Second, avoid giving service accounts interactive shells or human passwords—use /sbin/nologin for accounts that only run automated tasks. Third, maintain separate administrative accounts for humans and use privilege escalation only when necessary. Fourth, when copying users between systems, plan UID and GID allocation to avoid collisions and unexpected numeric owners. Concretely, audit /etc/passwd for unfamiliar system accounts and confirm their shells and home directories before granting any additional privileges. A common mistake is using a system account for daily administration; this blurs responsibility and increases risk. Takeaway: follow the principle of least privilege, limit audit surface by keeping secrets in shadow, and preserve clear separation between service and human accounts to maintain secure, auditable systems. Security practices for accounts means keep shadow root-only, use nologin for services, separate admin accounts, and plan uid/gid when migrating users.. fullNarratorScript:
Every action on a Linux system happens on behalf of a user. User accounts give each person or service a unique identity so the kernel can enforce permissions, log activity, and allocate resources. In this chapter you will learn how user accounts are defined, how the system maps human names to numerical IDs, and why sensitive data is separated into more secure files. We will examine the canonical /etc/passwd entry, explain each colon-separated field, and contrast that file with /etc/shadow where encrypted password hashes live. You will also learn how UIDs and GIDs drive ownership and permission checks, why system accounts use special shells like /sbin/nologin, and where personal configuration files live in a home directory. By the end you will be able to read a passwd line, interpret UID/GID ownership, locate common dotfiles, and decide whether an account is a system service account or a regular user. Think about one account on your system you can inspect safely; this chapter helps you understand what each field means and how to interpret ownership across systems.

In this set of objectives we focus on core skills you will practice. First, you'll explain the purpose and structure of user accounts: why each account exists, what metadata is stored, and how the operating system uses that information. Second, you'll learn to identify key fields in the /etc/passwd file, read them correctly, and understand the meaning of each colon-separated value. Third, you'll differentiate UIDs and GIDs: you will be able to state how numerical identifiers map to names and how the kernel uses numbers for permission checks. Fourth, you'll locate and interpret user-specific configuration files and directories such as home directories and common dotfiles. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competency by running commands and inspecting safe files. These skills let you audit accounts, trace file ownership, and troubleshoot permission issues with confidence.

This screen connects objectives to hands-on evidence. For explaining account structure, you will show a passwd line and annotate each field in your notes. For identifying /etc/passwd fields, you will run grep on your username and point out the username, placeholder, UID, GID, GECOS, home directory, and login shell. For differentiating UID and GID, you will read the id command output and note numeric IDs and group membership, and explain why a file may show a numeric owner on another system. For locating user configuration, you will list your home directory contents including hidden dotfiles, and open. bashrc or. profile to explain what customizations live there. Each card below maps the skill to a short verification step you can run safely on your machine. This makes the objectives actionable and prepares you for administrative tasks and troubleshooting.

A Linux user account is a system identity used to run commands, own files, and access resources. The account ties a human or service to a set of rights and a workspace, so every change can be attributed and access can be enforced. This matters because the kernel evaluates actions by UID and GID, not by username text. If accounts are poorly managed, auditing is harder and unauthorized actions can go unnoticed. A concrete example is creating a file: the file is recorded with numerical owner and group identifiers; when another system lacks the same user ID, the file owner may display only as a number. A common misconception is that the username alone governs permissions; in fact the kernel only uses the numerical ID. Another confusion is treating system service accounts like regular users; many service accounts have restricted shells to prevent interactive login. Takeaway: treat user accounts as auditable identities—use distinct administrative accounts for people, reserve system accounts for services, and inspect UID/GID when diagnosing ownership issues. Which account will you inspect first to confirm ownership on your host?

The /etc/passwd file is a plain-text table listing each account on the system. Each line has seven colon-separated fields that describe the account metadata. Let's walk through the canonical example line: johndoe:x:1001:1001:John Doe,,,:/home/johndoe:/bin/bash. The username is the login label you type. The second field is typically an x placeholder indicating password hashes live in /etc/shadow. The third field is the UID, the numerical identity the kernel uses. The fourth is the primary GID, tying the account to a default group. The fifth field, the GECOS or comment field, stores optional human-readable information like full name and contact. The sixth field sets the user's home directory and the seventh sets the login shell. A concrete step to practice is grep "$(whoami)" /etc/passwd and then explain each field aloud. A common misunderstanding is expecting sensitive data in passwd; instead, only a placeholder appears because the real secret is stored in the root-only shadow file. End by asking: can you name the seven fields for your account and explain the role of the UID? Reading /etc/passwd means seven fields: username, password placeholder, uid, gid, gecos, home directory, login shell — all colon-separated.. In practical terms, understand each colon-separated field with a real example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

UIDs and GIDs are core to how Linux enforces file permissions. When you open or modify a file, the kernel checks the process's effective UID and groups against the file's owner UID and group GID. If the effective UID matches the file owner, owner permissions apply; otherwise, if any of the process groups match the file group, group permissions apply; if neither, the world permissions apply. Concretely, run id to see your UID and supplementary groups; then create a simple file and observe ownership with ls -l. A common pitfall is assuming username strings are authoritative; ownership is numeric and the mapping to names depends on local /etc/passwd entries. Another scenario: you copy files between hosts and see only numeric owners. To resolve this, either recreate the same UID/GID on the destination or chown the files to existing users. Takeaway: always reason about numbers — UIDs and GIDs — when diagnosing permission mismatches. How would you fix a file owned by UID 1005 on a new host? UIDs, GIDs, and permission checks means kernel compares process uid/gids to file uid/gid values; names are resolved only for display.. In practical terms, how numerical ids determine ownership and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Linux distinguishes system accounts created for services from regular human user accounts. System accounts typically have UIDs below 1000 and are used by daemons like apache or mysql. They often have non-interactive shells such as /bin/nologin or /sbin/nologin to prevent direct login. Regular user accounts typically start at 1000 (or 500 on some distributions) and have home directories and interactive shells like /bin/bash. A practical example: an account with UID 2 or UID 0 is a system account; root is UID 0 and has full privileges. A common mistake is enabling interactive login for a service account; this increases risk and complicates audits. When you see a passwd entry with /sbin/nologin, understand it is intended for automated processes rather than human sessions. Takeaway: maintain strict separation—create separate regular administrator accounts for people and keep service accounts constrained. Which accounts on your system have shells set to nologin, and why were they configured that way? System accounts vs regular user accounts means system accounts (uids usually <1000) run services and use non-interactive shells; regular users have interactive shells and home directories.. In practical terms, uid ranges, shells, and intended use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A user's home directory, usually /home/username, is the personal workspace where files and configuration live. Hidden dotfiles like. bashrc,. profile, and. vimrc customize the shell and applications when a user logs in. Inspecting these files helps you troubleshoot environment problems or unexpected behavior. For example,. bashrc may set prompt customization and PATH additions;. profile can set environment variables that apply to login shells. A practical step is cd ~ and ls -a to list hidden files, then open a dotfile to note export statements or aliases. A common misconception is that dotfiles are system-wide; they are per-user and only affect that user's environment unless copied into /etc/profile or skeleton directories. As an administrator, you may need to check dotfiles when a user reports a broken shell or missing command. Takeaway: know where user-specific settings live and how they are applied during login so you can quickly diagnose environment issues. Home directories and dotfiles means home directories store user files and hidden dotfiles (.bashrc, .profile) that customize the user's shell and environment.. In practical terms, where user-specific configuration and environment settings live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are a few essential commands for inspecting your account and mapping numeric IDs. whoami prints your current username; id shows your UID, primary GID, and supplementary groups. Use grep "$(whoami)" /etc/passwd to display the passwd entry for your account. These commands give you both the human-readable name and the numeric IDs you need to reason about ownership and permissions. For example, after running id you might see uid=1001(johndoe) gid=1001(johndoe) groups=1001(johndoe),27(sudo). This tells you your numeric identity and that you are a member of the sudo group. A common trap is reading only names and ignoring the numeric values; always note the UID when diagnosing ownership. When you need to inspect the encrypted password entry, use sudo grep "$(whoami)" /etc/shadow but do so carefully—shadow contains hashes and should not be shared. Takeaway: these commands form a fast inspection workflow to answer who owns a file and what groups a user belongs to.
